citations.quote: As space engineering projects become more complex, MBSE (Model-Based Systems Engineering) practices have been gaining popularity to enforce consistency throughout the multiple facets of an integrated system. However, most such approaches are often confined to the top levels of systems engineering, leaving tooling gaps between the design and the implementation, integration, and testing phases, which can be the source of inconsistencies. Exceptions are few and typically proprietary, leaving limited freedom for customisation.

Building on previous work from N7 Space, this paper presents a comprehensive, V-shaped methodology integrating Capella and TASTE workflows into an end-to-end model-centric process for developing embedded software within complex systems. Capella is an opinionated MBSE tool, created by Thales to enforce the Arcadia framework, which structures the design process on multiple levels: Operational, System, Logical, and Physical; TASTE is a model-driven software development toolchain targeting heterogenous embedded systems, which centres its workflow around Data, Interface, and Deployment views. Both tools are Free and Open-Source Software.

This methodology exploits the parallels between entities in the two tools to rigorously link the design and implementation phases, enabling verification and validation activities based on simple diagram comparisons. Capella is first used to reason about the operational scenarios required to accomplish the chosen mission, then to consistently define the architectures of the system, its logical subsystems, and the physical components. The final products of the design stage are rigorously transitioned to TASTE, exploiting its SDL (Specification and Description Language) support to develop embedded software faithfully to the model. Finally, TASTE's integration with model-checking frameworks enables formal verification to be carried out on selected software requirements, whereas MSC (Message Sequence Chart) generation enables validation of its structure against the designs at multiple levels.

To illustrate the process, we report the resulting software architectures and their integration into the broader system of a student CubeSat project, where this method is currently being adopted to develop and test both flight and ground software, including TTMC, housekeeping, and mission functionalities. While we highlight its particular benefits to student projects, the method's exclusive reliance on open-source tools makes it easily adaptable to more complex use cases, and widely accessible regardless of financial and computational means.

Integration between Capella and TASTE was first proposed in [2] as a bridge plugin automating the generation of TASTE model files from a Capella model. This seminal work adopts a mapping mostly equivalent to the one we propose; however, it only bridges physical-level modelling in Capella with implementation activities in TASTE.

As illustrated in fig. 1, the workflows for all design levels mainly repeat the same core semantic pattern: breaking down higher-level Functions [ $ ^{*} $ FBD]/ $ ^{*} $ DFB]), breaking down higher-level Components [ $ ^{*} $ CBD]), allocating the former to the latter [ $ ^{*} $ AB]), defining component Modes and allocating Functions to either Modes or Transitions [MSM]), and finally representing all this information in a sequence-style diagram [ES]). These workflows should be driven by the realisation of higher-level FCs in the current level. Achieving this realisation is a core consistency principle of the Arcadia methodology enforced by Capella; however, in the process we propose, it is particularly important to adopt it as a design driver because of the implications in the verification and validation phases elaborated in section 3.3.

At the System Analysis level, we begin by defining the highlevel Functions to be performed by the System as a black box. This is done in a [SFBD] diagram. We also specify the FEs between the different Functions involved in accomplishing any given System Capability, and collate them in FCs that embody the Capability realisations. This, along with optionally the breakdown, is done in a [SDFB] diagram. Also optionally, if this level was preceded by a Capella Operational Analysis, [SDFB] diagrams can highlight FC realisations by laying out the leaf Functions involved in a FC at the System level and grouping them under their parent Functions which realise the Functions involved in the realised FC at the Operational level.

Third, we allocate the Functions to either the System or an Actor. This is done in a [SAB] diagram. We recommend starting from a complete view of all Functions and Actors, and cloning it into one view per Capability, only representing the subset of Functions and Actors involved in the FCs that realise it. This is generally helpful to improve readability, but particularly important in the proposed method: as illustrated in fig. 1 and detailed in section 3.3.3, these subset views will be involved in the acceptance-level verification activities at the

Fourth, we model the behaviour of the System as an FSM by specifying the Modes the System can assume, and connecting them through appropriate Transitions. At this level, we have found that allocating the Functions performed by the System to Modes, rather than to Transitions, results in a more intuitive semantic model. As this approach leaves Transitions free to allocate FEs, it represents the System continuously executing highlevel tasks for the entirety of its permanence in a given Mode; whenever a task or set of tasks is exhausted, a Transition is triggered to bring the System to its next Mode. Thanks to the relatively informal status of FSMs within Capella, a Transition-based Function allocation scheme can be adopted in subsequent levels (and will, in section 3.1.3) without any glaring inconsistency, i.e. without introducing any error flagged by Capella's model validation routine. Both these actions are done in a [MSM] diagram.

Finally, we represent all elements developed so far in a sequence format, which can also convey additional information such as informal timing, loops, branching, and notes. This is done in [ES] diagrams. Again, as with the Architectures, we recommend creating a separate [ES] diagram for each System Capability - especially since, unlike Architectures, [ES] diagrams are formally linked to System Capabilities. Each diagram should reproduce the FC(s) which realise the Capability, and state the Mode assumed by the System whenever it changes. Laying out the diagram this way creates a direct equivalence between Capella's [ES] and TASTE's MSC, enabling their comparison as a verification activity as detailed in section 3.3.3.

We begin the Logical Architecture level by realising the System Capabilities, System Functions, and System Actors into Logical Capabilities, Logical Functions, and Logical Actors, which can conveniently be done through Capella's automatic transition features. Function Breakdown/Data Flow Next, similarly to the previous level, we break down the highlevel Functions (those "inherited" from the System level) into Functions appropriate for allocation to subsystems.

At the Logical level, the System turns from a black box to a grey box, where more granular entities can be discerned as Logical Components. Second, therefore, we break down the System into its constituting Logical Components representing subsystems. This is done in a [LCBD] diagram. Capella does support nesting Logical Components with multiple hierarchical tiers, e.g. considering "segments", "platforms", "modules", etc. and then subsystems; however, that is beyond the scope of this method. If relevant to a project, we recommend shifting that complexity above subsystem entities upstream in the modelling cascade, for instance by adopting a federated model (model-of-models) structure. On the other hand, all complexity below subsystem entities is elaborated at the Physical level, as detailed in section 3.1.3.

Just like previously, we begin the Physical Architecture level by realising the Logical Capabilities, Logical Functions, Logical Actors, and Logical Components into Physical Capabilities, Physical Functions, Physical Actors, and Behaviour PCs, which can conveniently be done through Capella's automatic transition features. Function Breakdown/Data Flow Next, similarly to the previous level, we break down the medium-level Functions (those "inherited" from the Logical level) into Functions appropriate for allocation to components - where "component" is a generic name for a Physical-level leaf entity, similarly to "subsystem" at the Logical level.

At the Physical level, the System turns from a grey box to a white box, where all entities can be discerned as PCs. Second, therefore, we break down the System into its constituting PCs representing components and component groups. This is done in a [PCBD] diagram. However, unlike at the previous level, two types of PC are envisioned in Capella: Behaviour PCs and Node PCs; in the context of this method, we map the former to software, and the latter to hardware.

Third, we allocate the broken-down Functions to the broken-down Behaviour PCs, and the broken-down Behaviour PCs to the broken-down Node PCs. Both these actions are done in a [PAB] diagram. Once again, we recommend starting from a complete view of all Functions and PCs within the System, and cloning it into one view per Capability, only representing the subset of Functions and PCs involved in the FCs that realise it.

At this level, as it is the closest to the implementation, the [ES] representation is not the final step; after that is done, we formally define the Interfaces between components and the Data exchanged through them. This is done across [PAB] and [CII] diagrams.

There, we create an Interface for every synchronous call-return Component Exchange pair or asynchronous call Component Exchange, and appropriately connect the relevant Flow Ports to it: providing it for the In direction; requiring it for the Out direction. We also create Exchange Items representing the parametres passed through each interface, and allocate one to the other accordingly. Due to limitations of TASTE Interfaces, we recommend allocating at most one parametre to each interface, and "packing" all necessary data points into a suitable data structure as part of the next step.

Finally, we specify the types of said parameters in a [CDB] diagram. This is done by creating the required Types (and optionally Literals, as in the case of Enumerations), and connecting them to the previously-defined Exchange Items through Exchange Item Element relationships. We represent data structures as Classes: for simple ones, we allocate one Property per primitive field; for more complex ones, we can also Aggregate simpler Classes.

This phase is performed across the Capella diagrams and TASTE views outlined in table 3: as illustrated in fig.1, this crossing of tooling boundaries mainly consists of populating TASTE views with the content specified in the relevant Capella diagram - and, thanks to the work done in section 3.1.3, this is largely trivial.

Generally, for each TASTE Function, this is implemented by following the individual steps specified in [PAB] as Capella Functions allocated to Behaviour PCs, in the order defined by their FEs. We recommend implementing as much logic as possible in SDL Functions, and only outsourcing thin hardware interfaces to a dedicated Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) Function implemented in C/C++. Taking advantage of one of TASTE's cornerstone features, implementing different Functions in different languages is possible and envisioned by this method. However, because most of TASTE's more advanced features rely on formal SDL Implementations, we recommend writing an alternative SDL Implementation for each non-SDL Function, which should mock the behaviour of the actual, non-SDL Implementation.
